caseStudies.title: Messenger Archive & Semantic Search
caseStudies.problem: Search text and transcribed audio by meaning in a private message archive.
caseStudies.context: A personal project that separates message import, transcription and indexing so each step can be retried.
caseStudies.architecture: Rust loads message records through MTProto. PostgreSQL stores records and transcription jobs. A Python worker runs Whisper, and a Rust indexer stores embeddings in Qdrant. An MCP interface exposes search.
challenges: Parallel workers can encounter jobs that another worker already claims.
The vector store and the indexing checkpoint are separate systems.
decisions: Use PostgreSQL row-level locks with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED to let workers skip conflicting rows.
Map each vector upsert to a deterministic UUIDv5 ID.
Advance the index checkpoint after the vector write succeeds.
reliability: A retry can repeat a vector write to the same point ID. Unrelated side effects need their own deduplication.
A crash between stages can leave work to replay. Progress is tracked at each completed stage.
results: Combines message and transcript search in an MCP interface.

provenance.summary: Independent personal project. The diagram describes software components and contains no example messages or account records.

caseStudies.title: EntityLocker — Row-Level Entity Concurrency Utility
caseStudies.problem: Explore how Java threads can coordinate by an entity key within one process.
caseStudies.context: EntityLocker is an independent Java utility with JUnit cases for several locking behaviours.
caseStudies.architecture: A concurrent map associates entity IDs with reentrant lock objects. A thread-local value records the current acquisition order and rejects a lower nested ID. Registry removal is attempted when a critical section exits.
challenges: Nested key acquisition can create dependency cycles.
Retiring a key safely requires coordination with both current holders and contenders.
decisions: Use one ordered key type and reject decreasing acquisitions on the same thread.
Keep the lock registry inside each EntityLocker instance.
reliability: Tests cover same-key access, reentrancy, timeouts and rejection of decreasing lock order.
Registry retirement needs additional stress testing. Separate instances or processes do not share these locks.
results: Illustrates JVM-local keyed locking and why safe reclamation needs separate verification.

provenance.summary: Public source and JUnit tests for a Java locking experiment maintained by Denis Stepulenok.

caseStudies.title: RustShot Desktop Capture
caseStudies.problem: Capture screenshots across different desktop environments with a common command-line interface.
caseStudies.context: RustShot is an independent Rust utility for Windows, Linux and macOS.
caseStudies.architecture: Platform-specific adapters acquire an image and send it to the requested output destination. Linux Wayland can use the desktop portal. Windows also supports screen recording.
challenges: Operating systems expose different capture capabilities.
Desktop portal workflows depend on the caller’s desktop session and permissions.
decisions: Document platform support separately for screenshots, region selection and recording.
Keep capture and output handling separate.
reliability: Repository tests cover capture helpers and output behaviour. Live desktop checks depend on the platform.
results: Provides screenshot capture on three desktop platforms and documents their feature differences.

provenance.summary: Public RustShot capture guide and source maintained by Denis Stepulenok.

architectureDiagrams.title: Semantic Search & MCP Integration
architectureDiagrams.label: Personal archive with message import, row-level job claiming, transcription, vector indexing and MCP search.
architectureDiagrams.summary: A personal archive with separate import, transcription and vector indexing stages. Retries can replay an upsert to the same point ID.

nodes.title: Messenger API (MTProto)
nodes.responsibility: Provides incremental message history and voice attachments subject to upstream rate limits.
nodes.tradeoffs: Rate-limited upstream API requires persistent cursor checkpoints to avoid costly full re-syncs.

nodes.title: Sync Service (Rust)
nodes.responsibility: Fetches history with exponential/flood-wait backoff and stores raw messages in PostgreSQL.
nodes.tradeoffs: Rust async runtime handles long-running sync sessions with predictable memory footprint.

nodes.title: PostgreSQL Store & Queue
nodes.detail: Claim available rows using row-level locks
nodes.responsibility: Workers claim transcription jobs in PostgreSQL with row-level locks. SKIP LOCKED lets a worker select other eligible rows while locks are held.
nodes.tradeoffs: Available rows can be claimed out of arrival order when earlier jobs are locked.

nodes.title: Transcription Worker (Python)
nodes.responsibility: A Python worker runs Whisper on claimed audio and stores the transcript for indexing.
nodes.tradeoffs: Jobs need retry or recovery rules for work that stops before completion.

nodes.title: Batch Indexer (Rust)
nodes.responsibility: The indexer assigns a deterministic vector ID and advances its checkpoint after the upsert succeeds.
nodes.tradeoffs: Writes can be replayed after a crash. The vector store and checkpoint do not share an atomic transaction.

nodes.title: Vector Store (Qdrant)
nodes.responsibility: Stores semantic embeddings keyed by deterministic UUIDv5 identifiers derived from message identity.
nodes.tradeoffs: Deterministic IDs avoid duplicate entries when the same vector is written again after a restart.

nodes.title: MCP Server (stdio / HTTP)
nodes.responsibility: Exposes semantic search and thread retrieval tools to LLM assistants over Model Context Protocol.
nodes.tradeoffs: Read-only query tools isolate LLM agents from direct database or session credentials.

provenance.summary: Independent personal project. The diagram describes software components and contains no example messages or account records.

architectureDiagrams.title: JVM-Local Entity Locking
architectureDiagrams.label: JVM-local keyed locking with a lock registry, lock acquisition, action execution and attempted registry retirement.
architectureDiagrams.summary: EntityLocker explores keyed locking among Java threads in one process. The code orders nested acquisition and attempts to retire idle registry entries.

nodes.title: Concurrent Caller Threads
nodes.detail: Threads in one JVM pass an entity key
nodes.responsibility: Threads using the same EntityLocker instance supply the key and code they wish to run.
nodes.tradeoffs: The lock registry is local to one instance. Other instances and processes are outside its scope.

nodes.title: Concurrent Lock Registry
nodes.detail: Look up a lock object by ID
nodes.responsibility: ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent associates a present key with a lock object.
nodes.tradeoffs: Safe retirement also requires coordination with the lock holders and contenders.

nodes.title: Per-ID Reentrant Lock
nodes.detail: Reentrant lock with an optional timeout
nodes.responsibility: The utility checks nested ID order within the calling thread, then uses a reentrant lock for blocking or timed acquisition.
nodes.tradeoffs: The ordering check applies to nested calls through the utility. Other locks can still participate in dependency cycles.

nodes.title: Protected Critical Section
nodes.detail: Run the action and release the lock
nodes.responsibility: When acquisition succeeds, the utility runs the caller’s action and releases the lock in a finally block.
nodes.tradeoffs: Rollback, where needed, relies on the resources or application code used by the action.

nodes.title: Registry Retirement
nodes.detail: Attempt to remove unused registry entries
nodes.responsibility: The implementation tries to retire an entry before releasing its current lock.
nodes.tradeoffs: Acquisition and retirement can overlap. Testing safe replacement requires schedules where both operations compete.

provenance.summary: Public source and JUnit tests for a Java locking experiment maintained by Denis Stepulenok.

architectureDiagrams.title: Transactional Outbox & Idempotent Event Consumer
architectureDiagrams.label: Educational outbox flow from a local database transaction through publication, delivery and duplicate handling.
architectureDiagrams.summary: An educational reference for committing an event with application data and relaying it to a broker. Repeated publication is possible, so consumers need a duplicate-handling strategy.

nodes.title: Domain Service (Java / Spring)
nodes.detail: Write business data and an outbox entry
nodes.responsibility: Use one local database transaction to update business data and persist the intended event.
nodes.tradeoffs: Atomicity covers this database transaction. The later broker publication is a separate operation.

nodes.title: Relational DB + Outbox Table
nodes.detail: Persist an event in the local transaction
nodes.responsibility: Make each committed event available to a relay, with a stable identifier.
nodes.tradeoffs: The outbox retains a pending event when the relay is unavailable. Broker delivery follows separate configuration.

nodes.title: Outbox Relay Publisher
nodes.detail: Publish pending events to the broker
nodes.responsibility: Read pending rows, publish to the broker and record progress after acknowledgement.
nodes.tradeoffs: A crash after publication but before recording progress can make the relay publish again.

nodes.title: Message Broker (Kafka / AMQP)
nodes.responsibility: Buffer and deliver events according to the broker configuration.
nodes.tradeoffs: At-least-once delivery can repeat messages. Delivery settings and failure behaviour vary by broker.

nodes.title: Idempotent Consumer
nodes.detail: Handle repeats with an event ID
nodes.responsibility: Deduplicate effects within a defined boundary, for example by writing a processed event ID and a local state change in one transaction.
nodes.tradeoffs: Other effects need their own mechanism. A database deduplication record does not protect an unrelated external call.

nodes.title: Retry & Dead-Letter Queue
nodes.responsibility: Retain failed messages for inspection after the configured retry policy is exhausted.
nodes.tradeoffs: Replaying a failed message still requires a duplicate-handling strategy.

provenance.summary: Independent reference design for teaching a general engineering pattern.

architectureDiagrams.title: Resilient Asynchronous Job Queue & Backpressure
architectureDiagrams.label: Educational asynchronous job flow from submission and claim through bounded execution, output publication and monitoring.
architectureDiagrams.summary: An educational reference for accepting jobs, constraining worker concurrency and publishing completed outputs.

nodes.title: Stateless API Frontend
nodes.responsibility: Authenticates requests, enqueues work asynchronously, and returns a job correlation ID immediately.
nodes.tradeoffs: Keeps request threads fast and predictable instead of blocking on long-running background work.

nodes.title: Persistent Work Queue
nodes.responsibility: Persist queued work and record a worker’s claim before execution.
nodes.tradeoffs: Retries and expired claims may allow a job to run again. Make effects safe to repeat.

nodes.title: Bounded Worker Pool
nodes.responsibility: Use a bounded worker pool to apply backpressure and keep job execution within configured limits.
nodes.tradeoffs: Higher concurrency increases resource use. Backpressure moves waiting time into the queue.

nodes.title: Publish Completed Outputs
nodes.responsibility: Write a temporary output and publish it with a replacement operation where the storage system supports it.
nodes.tradeoffs: Atomic replacement is storage-dependent. A queue acknowledgement is a separate operation.

nodes.title: Health, Metrics & Cleanup
nodes.responsibility: Monitor queue depth, job age and failure counts to identify delays or repeated errors.
nodes.tradeoffs: Signals need thresholds and investigation. Durability depends on storage and retry behaviour.

provenance.summary: Independent reference design for teaching a general engineering pattern.

engineeringConcepts.name: Idempotency
engineeringConcepts.description: Repeating an operation has the same effect within a defined boundary. A stable key can prevent duplicate records without covering unrelated effects.

engineeringConcepts.name: Eventual Consistency
engineeringConcepts.description: Separate stores may disagree while updates are in progress. Retries and reconciliation can help them converge when the changes are applied.

engineeringConcepts.name: Message Delivery Guarantees
engineeringConcepts.description: At-least-once delivery can repeat a message. Exactly-once processing requires a clearly defined transaction and effect boundary.

engineeringConcepts.name: Failure Handling
engineeringConcepts.description: Recover from transient faults through bounded retries, and expose persistent failures for inspection or replay.

engineeringConcepts.name: Distributed Coordination
engineeringConcepts.description: Threads in one JVM can share a lock. Multiple processes need a coordination mechanism with its own failure model.

engineeringConcepts.name: Cache Consistency
engineeringConcepts.description: Cached data can become stale. Expiry, invalidation and refresh policies determine when it becomes consistent with its source.

engineeringConcepts.name: Observability
engineeringConcepts.description: Logs, metrics and traces help explain behaviour and investigate failures.

engineeringConcepts.name: Security
engineeringConcepts.description: Use authentication, authorisation, appropriate data handling and a documented threat model to protect access.

articles.title: Java Concurrency and Keyed Entity Locking
articles.author: Denis Stepulenok
articles.provenance: Independent engineering write-up grounded in the public stden/EntityLocker repository; no employer code or production metrics.
articles.summary: Designing per-entity mutex synchronization in JVM memory using ConcurrentHashMap, per-key ReentrantLock instances, and canonical key ordering — plus an honest look at lock-registry eviction races.

sections.heading: Why Keyed Locking Instead of a Global Lock
paragraphs: When in-memory workers update domain aggregates keyed by entity ID, coarse synchronization on a shared collection serializes unrelated entities and limits throughput.

A keyed lock registry maintains one ReentrantLock per active key in a ConcurrentHashMap so threads operating on distinct IDs proceed concurrently while threads targeting the same ID coordinate cleanly.

sections.heading: Preventing Deadlocks Across Multiple Keys
paragraphs: If Thread A locks entity 10 then 20 while Thread B locks 20 then 10, lock-order inversion triggers a classic deadlock.

Sorting keys canonically before acquisition establishes a strict global total order across threads. Because ReentrantLock is reentrant per thread, deduplicating identical keys or acquiring in ascending comparable order eliminates two-key cycles.

tradeoffs: Per-key in-memory locks avoid database round-trips for single-JVM coordination, but provide zero protection across multiple application replicas (distributed workloads require database row locks or external leases).
Keeping lock entries forever leaks memory on unbounded ID spaces, whereas eager eviction introduces race conditions if not synchronized atomically with reference counts.
limitations: In public stden/EntityLocker, CountLock maintains an enter counter separately from map removal, creating a documented non-atomic race under simultaneous acquire and eviction.
EntityLocker includes JUnit 4 tests in src/test/java/EntityLockerTest.java but does not yet configure an automated GitHub Actions CI workflow.

reproducibleExperiment.summary: Clone stden/EntityLocker and run its Maven/JUnit test suite locally under two concurrent stress scenarios (same-key contention vs swapped multi-key acquisition).

articles.title: Kafka Consumer Behaviour, Idempotency, and the Transactional Outbox
articles.author: Denis Stepulenok
articles.provenance: Independent educational analysis of Apache Kafka delivery semantics and outbox patterns; contains no employer topology or proprietary broker configuration.
articles.summary: Why consumer rebalances and dual writes break naive event pipelines, how partitioned key ordering interacts with retry topics, and where transactional outbox plus idempotent consumers restore safety.

sections.heading: At-Least-Once Delivery Across Consumer Rebalances
paragraphs: When a Kafka consumer processes a batch, writes side effects to a database, and crashes before committing offsets, the next rebalance replays those records to another consumer instance.
Even with enable.auto.commit=false and manual acknowledgment, network timeouts or poll interval expiry (max.poll.interval.ms) can evict a consumer mid-batch and cause duplicate delivery.

sections.heading: Avoiding Dual Writes with Transactional Outbox + Idempotency
paragraphs: Updating local state and calling producer.send() in separate steps creates a dual-write window where one succeeds and the other fails. Writing both the domain change and an outbox row inside one ACID database transaction closes that window.

On the consumer side, persisting a deterministic event_id in a deduplication table (with a unique constraint) in the same local transaction guarantees idempotent state transitions even across broker retries or consumer rebalances.

tradeoffs: Non-blocking retry topics avoid stalling healthy keys behind a single poison pill, but weaken strict per-key ordering while a failing key sits in a delayed retry topic.
CDC-based outbox publishing (e.g., log tailing) reduces polling load compared to database polling relays, at the cost of extra connector operational complexity.
limitations: Deduplication tables grow over time and require bounded retention aligned with Kafka topic retention or downstream replay windows.
Examples are vendor-neutral educational patterns and exclude employer-specific topic names, partition counts, or SLAs.

reproducibleExperiment.summary: Verify idempotent deduplication in any local PostgreSQL instance by simulating a replayed event batch inside a transaction that aborts after state mutation but before offset acknowledgement.
commands: CREATE TABLE processed_events (event_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, processed_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL);
Run duplicate INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (event_id) DO NOTHING and verify row count stays 1.

articles.title: PostgreSQL Row-Level Locking for Concurrent Worker Queues
articles.author: Denis Stepulenok
articles.provenance: Independent PostgreSQL concurrency note using reproducible standard SQL; excludes employer schemas and non-public benchmarks.
articles.summary: Comparing SELECT FOR UPDATE, NOWAIT, and FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED when implementing multi-worker job claims on top of a relational database.

sections.heading: Blocking vs Non-Blocking Claim Queries
paragraphs: Naive SELECT followed by UPDATE lets two workers claim the same queued row concurrently. Adding FOR UPDATE prevents double claims, yet causes subsequent workers to block waiting on the first worker's transaction commit.
Adding SKIP LOCKED allows each concurrent worker session to atomically claim the next unlocked eligible row without waiting on rows locked by active transactions.
sections.code:
WITH next_job AS (
  SELECT id FROM job_queue
  WHERE status = 'PENDING' AND run_at <= CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
  ORDER BY run_at, id
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
  LIMIT 1
)
UPDATE job_queue q
SET status = 'CLAIMED', claimed_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
FROM next_job
WHERE q.id = next_job.id
RETURNING q.id;

tradeoffs: SKIP LOCKED simplifies transactional enqueue-with-domain-state without operating a dedicated broker, but high update churn creates dead tuples requiring tuned autovacuum.
Holding transactions open during external HTTP calls exhausts database connections; fast claim-to-LEASED transactions with visibility timeouts scale much better.
limitations: Relational queues do not match dedicated log brokers like Apache Kafka for multi-consumer fan-out or high-throughput event replay.
Reproducible experiment tests lock semantics rather than production cluster sizing.

reproducibleExperiment.summary: Open two psql sessions on the same PostgreSQL database, execute the CTE claim without committing in Session 1, and observe Session 2 claim row 2 immediately.
commands: Session 1: BEGIN; SELECT id FROM job_queue WHERE status = 'PENDING' ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1;
Session 2: BEGIN; SELECT id FROM job_queue WHERE status = 'PENDING' ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1;

articles.title: Rust and Model Context Protocol (MCP) for Local Archive Retrieval
articles.author: Denis Stepulenok
articles.provenance: Based on independent personal archive experimentation and public modules in stden/pythorust_tg.
articles.summary: Structuring read-only stdio MCP tools in front of a hybrid lexical and vector retrieval index so coding or research agents inspect narrow evidence without exfiltrating raw archives.

sections.heading: Why Expose Narrow Read-Only Tools Instead of Raw File Access
paragraphs: Giving an LLM agent unrestricted filesystem or database access mixes unrelated personal records into context windows and increases accidental leakage.
A narrow read-only MCP tool contract (search metadata filters, top-k chunk retrieval with explicit source IDs, and bounded payload size) enforces least privilege at the boundary.

sections.heading: Separating Indexing from Deterministic Query Execution
paragraphs: Hybrid retrieval pairs exact keyword filters with dense vector similarity so proper nouns and identifiers do not disappear in semantic-only matching.
Keeping ingestion idempotent and schema-validated ensures incremental updates do not corrupt existing embeddings or citations.

tradeoffs: Local stdio MCP servers avoid hosting credentials or exposing public network endpoints, while trading away remote multi-user sharing.
Chunk size optimization balances citation precision against surrounding conversational context.
limitations: Independent personal tooling without public retrieval recall/precision benchmark datasets.
No personal archive records, prompts, or private identifiers are published.

articles.title: Automated Testing, Deterministic Validation Gates, and Software Reliability
articles.author: Denis Stepulenok
articles.provenance: Grounded in public quality gates in stden/CV, SonarQubeChecker, RustShot, and public JUnit experience.
articles.summary: Treating static HTML, ATS PDFs, confidentiality scanning, and WCAG accessibility as machine-checked build gates rather than manual post-hoc checklists.

sections.heading: Shifting Verification into Reproducible Pipeline Stages
paragraphs: Manual checklists fail under time pressure: broken relative links under /CV/, overflowing mobile layouts, clipped PDF text, or unintended file inclusions slip through unless checked automatically on every change.
Building an explicit allowlist staging step before validation ensures that deployment tests inspect the exact artifact set destined for production rather than stale working-tree leftovers.

sections.heading: Combining Fast Unit Checks with Real Browser & PDF Inspection
paragraphs: Fast Node unit tests verify pure domain logic (JSON schemas, locale key parity, confidentiality regexes, and matching rules) in under a second.
Playwright browser checks and Poppler PDF bounds verification then validate real rendering, no-JavaScript fallbacks, keyboard focus, and WCAG 2.1 AA contrast across desktop and mobile viewports.

tradeoffs: Strict allowlist staging rejects unexpected files immediately, requiring explicit manifest updates whenever a new output format is introduced.
End-to-end browser and PDF checks take several seconds in CI compared to pure unit tests, so keeping clean separation preserves fast local feedback.
limitations: Automated gates verify structural correctness, link integrity, contrast, and policy patterns; domain accuracy of claims still requires human review.

reproducibleExperiment.summary: Run the staged artifact check, Node unit suite, and Playwright accessibility checks locally inside stden/CV.
